title: Object-Oriented Swift: Accounts
hints: Classes are reference types — the dictionary stores references you can mutate through.
`SavingsAccount` overrides `withdraw` and calls `super.withdraw` after its own check.
`guard balance - amount >= 100 else { return false }; return super.withdraw(amount)`.
jsBridge: Classic OOP in Swift: a base class with `private(set)` state, a `final` subclass overriding `withdraw`. It's familiar from JS classes. The Swift-specific parts are `override`, `final` and compile-time access control.

compass.q: How would JS `#balance` interact with a subclass that needs to read it? What does Swift's `private(set)` allow instead?
Inheritance vs composition (`Account` holding a `WithdrawalPolicy`): which is easier to extend with new account types?
`override func withdraw` calling `super.withdraw`: what if the base changes its rules?
Should money-handling types be classes at all, or actors, given concurrent access?
